Hello, I’m GPTREI, your requirements elicitation assistant. I’ll be gathering detailed information about the University of Puget Sound courseware system so we can clearly understand what’s needed and what success should look like.

Before we begin, are you aligned with this interview scope, or do you expect something different?

Yes, that sounds aligned with what we need. We’re looking to understand how the courseware should support courses, assignments, learning materials, discussions, and grading for students, professors, and administrators. If we can get clarity on those workflows and any special university needs, that would be the right scope.
To start off, could you please introduce yourself and your connection to this project?

I’m speaking as someone representing the university’s academic side, with a focus on how faculty and students will actually use the system day to day. I’m involved because we need this platform to support teaching, course management, and student access in a way that fits our practices.
Thank you. Could you describe the current process or system you use for managing courses, assignments, learning materials, discussions, and grades?

Right now, the process is a mix of separate tools and a lot of manual coordination. Some faculty use the LMS for certain course functions, but there are still email threads, shared drives, and manual grade handling that make everything feel disconnected. It works, but it’s not as smooth or consistent as we’d like.
What current processes do you want to change or improve, or what features do you hope to get from this project?

We’d like to bring those pieces into one coherent system so course information, materials, discussions, assignments, and grades are all in one place. I’d also want it to be easier for students to find what they need and for professors to manage a course without bouncing between tools. Better collaboration and a cleaner experience are the main goals.
Based on your description, do you think administrative tools for managing users, courses, and permissions should also be included?

Yes, definitely. We’ll need administrative tools for things like managing users, setting course access, and handling permissions, because the system can’t work well if faculty and staff have to do those things manually. I’m not sure yet how much control should be centralized versus left to departments, though.

So far, I understand the main features/functions as: course information, learning materials, discussions, assignments, grades, and administrative tools for users, courses, and permissions. Are there any other features you would like to see in this project?

I think those are the core pieces, but I’d also expect some kind of announcements or class updates feature so instructors can communicate quickly with students. If it’s feasible, basic notifications would be helpful too, so people don’t miss assignment changes or new discussion activity. Beyond that, I’d want the system to be flexible enough to refine as we learn more.
Which of these features should be the highest priority for the first version of the system?

For the first version, I’d prioritize course information, assignments, learning materials, grades, and the basic administrative controls needed to get courses set up and access managed. Discussions and notifications are important too, but I’d treat them as next in line if we need to stage the rollout. The main goal early on is to make sure teaching and course administration can happen reliably in one place.
Please elaborate on what you want the course information feature to accomplish.

It should give students a clear, central place to see the essentials for each course, like the syllabus, meeting times, instructor details, and key deadlines. For faculty, it should be easy to update that information when anything changes. Ideally, it also makes it obvious whether a course is current, upcoming, or archived.
Could you describe more about how instructors should update course information when changes happen?

Instructors should be able to edit course details themselves without needing support from IT for routine changes. If they update a meeting time, deadline, or syllabus link, I’d expect that change to appear quickly and be visible to students right away. It would also be helpful if the system kept some history of changes, but I’m not sure yet how much auditing we need.
How should the system handle the history of those course information changes?

I think it should at least keep a record of what changed, who changed it, and when, so we can troubleshoot if something goes wrong or there’s confusion later. It would be useful if we could view prior versions of important course details, but I don’t think every minor edit needs to be heavily exposed to regular users. The main thing is having enough history for accountability and recovery.
Please elaborate on what you want the assignments feature to accomplish.

Assignments should let instructors create, publish, and update coursework with due dates, instructions, and any attached files or links. Students should be able to see what is assigned, what is coming up, and what has already been turned in. It would also be helpful if the feature supports submission tracking, so instructors can tell what has been received and what still needs attention.
Could you describe more about what you want students to do when they submit an assignment?

Students should be able to upload a file or enter text directly, depending on the assignment type. After submitting, they ought to get a clear confirmation that the work was received, and ideally they should be able to see whether they submitted on time. If resubmissions are allowed, the system should make that straightforward too.
Please elaborate on what you want the learning materials feature to accomplish.

Learning materials should give instructors a simple way to post readings, slides, links, and other course resources in one place for students to access anytime. Students should be able to find materials by course and preferably see what’s new without hunting through emails or separate sites. It would also help if the materials are organized clearly by topic or week, but that may depend on how each instructor wants to structure the course.
How should students and instructors find and organize those learning materials within a course?

I’d want them grouped in a way that makes sense for the course, usually by week, module, or topic, and instructors should be able to choose the structure that fits best. Students should be able to browse that structure easily and also search within the course if they’re looking for a specific file or reading. If something gets moved or renamed, it should still be easy to find, so the organization needs to be fairly stable.
Please elaborate on what you want the grades feature to accomplish.

The grades feature should let instructors enter and update grades for assignments and other graded work, and let students view their own results in a clear way. Students should be able to see individual scores, maybe some overall course total, and understand what work is still pending grading. It would also be important that grade visibility is controlled so students only see their own information and instructors can manage grades for the courses they teach.
Could you describe more about how grading should work when instructors enter or update grades?

Instructors should be able to enter grades manually, and ideally update them after review if there’s been a correction. The system should save who changed a grade and when, since grades are sensitive and we may need to explain changes later. If possible, it should also reduce mistakes by making it easy to edit individual scores without disrupting the rest of the gradebook.
Please elaborate on what you want the administrative tools feature to accomplish.

Administrative tools should let system administrators manage users, courses, and basic courseware settings without needing technical help every time. They should be able to add or remove accounts, assign roles, and set up course access so the right people see the right courses. It would also be useful for them to support and troubleshoot the system when something goes wrong, though the exact level of control may still need to be defined.
How should permissions be structured between administrators, faculty, and students?

Permissions should be role-based, with administrators having the broadest control over accounts, course setup, and system settings. Faculty should control the content, assignments, discussions, and grades for the courses they teach, while students should mainly have access to their enrolled courses and their own submissions and grades. We’d want to avoid people seeing or changing information outside their role, especially when it comes to grades and course administration.
Which other stakeholders do you think have valuable insights into the project, and whose needs need to be considered, and why?

Besides students, faculty, and system administrators, I think academic advisors and department staff would have useful input because they often deal with enrollment questions and course coordination. Library staff might also matter if the system is going to link heavily to readings or course resources. I’d also include accessibility services or disability support, since the system needs to work well for all students, not just the typical case.
What would you consider a successful deployment of this courseware system?

A successful deployment would mean the system is stable, easy for people to adopt, and actually supports teaching and learning better than the current process. In practice, students and faculty should be able to use it for everyday course work without a lot of confusion or support tickets, and administrators should feel confident managing it. I’d also want to see that it can be refined after launch based on real feedback, rather than being considered finished on day one.

To summarize, we discussed a unified courseware system for course information, assignments, learning materials, grades, and administrative controls, with discussions and notifications as later priorities. We also covered course editing history, role-based permissions, and stakeholders such as advisors, department staff, library staff, and accessibility services. Is there anything else you would like to add?

One thing I’d add is that the system should be reliable and simple enough that it doesn’t create extra work for faculty or students. If there are notification features later, it would be helpful if they’re configurable so people aren’t overwhelmed. Otherwise, that summary sounds right to me.
